title: Send the read back to the worker that ran the last one
impact: `ReaderPool._dispatch` advanced its scan cursor on every attempt, so back-to-back reads deliberately rotated across the whole pool even when it was idle. Reader workers are not interchangeable resources: each is an isolate with its own SQLite connection and page cache, its own entry in that connection's C statement cache, its own Dart schema cache and cell buffer, and its own OS thread. Round-robin therefore made all four workers independently pay for warm state the first one had already built — a fixed cost per (statement, worker) pair, invisible to every benchmark in the repo because they all execute one statement thousands of times, and very visible to an application that opens a screen, runs a query four or five times and moves on. Starting the scan at the slot that served the previous read instead of the next one is worth -32.2% on a statement's first four executions, -21.8% on its first eight and -13.2% on its first thirty-two, decaying to -1.6% by the eight-thousandth — the monotonic decay the experiment was gated on, and direct confirmation the mechanism is warm-up rather than anything per-read. A busy preferred slot still walks forward, so concurrency is untouched: four concurrent reads (+1.3%), eight against a four-worker pool (+0.2%) and a 60,000-slot result that ends its worker every sample (-0.4%) are all neutral and sign-flip between collections. Peak RSS falls where the win is (27.0 -> 26.0 MB, 29.5 -> 28.2 MB) because one worker now holds once what four held four times. `selectBytes` deliberately keeps the old rotation: exp 185's `JSON buffer reclaim` release guard rejected the first, fully-sticky version at 6.2 MB against a 512 KB budget, because exp 183's `json_buf` shrink is driven by a later small read arriving on the same connection, and stickiness never sends one to the three workers a large burst had grown. Three lines of dispatch change plus that opt-out, no public API change, three new dispatch tests. Twenty-four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes in two collections.
